whyItMatters: Audited hand-hygiene compliance on the two medical wards sits at 52% against a 90% target, and the gap is not knowledge — staff can recite the WHO 'five moments'. It is behaviour under pressure. Compliance collapses at the moments that matter most: 41% before patient contact and 38% during the 08:00-11:00 round, when the ward is busiest and a missed moment is most likely to transmit infection. Two things make the moment harder than it needs to be: alcohol-gel dispensers are sometimes empty at the bed bay, and senior clinicians model the behaviour inconsistently, so juniors take their cue from a mixed signal. Naming a measurable target — compliance at the before-contact moment, on the round, with gel always within reach — keeps later phases focused on the few changes that move the audited number rather than on repeating training everyone has already had.
objective: More staff clean their hands at the moments that matter — especially before patient contact and during the morning round — so audited compliance rises toward the 90% target and holds there.

keyResults.kr: Eliminate empty bed-bay dispensers at the point of care
keyResults.metric: Bed-bay dispensers found stocked on spot check

gapLog.content: The audit is direct observation (n=300 opportunities), so the Hawthorne effect may inflate the measured 52% — true unobserved compliance is unknown.
The 6-of-56 empty-dispenser finding reflects routine stocking, not a one-off supply gap.
Confirm who owns bed-bay dispenser refills at ward level — staff describe hunting for a refill, suggesting no clear point-of-care restocking routine.
Healthcare assistants were excluded from the last training and are not separately audited during personal care, so their baseline compliance is unknown.
